title: Acting DS of Windhoek v Kamunoko (HC-MD-CIV-MOT-GEN-2024-00293) [2025] NAHCMD 324
text:
REPUBLIC OF NAMIBIA
HIGH COURT OF NAMIBIA MAIN DIVISION, WINDHOEK
JUDGMENT
	Case No: HC-MD-CIV-MOT-GEN-2024/00293

In the matter between:
THE ACTING DEPUTY SHERIFF FOR THE 
DISTRICT OF WINDHOEK	APPLICANT
and
DANIEL KUDUMO KAMUNOKO	 1st RESPONDENT
SCHAMEERAH COURT NO. SEVEN CC	 2nd RESPONDENT
Neutral citation:	The Acting Deputy Sheriff for the District of Windhoek v Kamunoko (HC-MD-CIV-MOT-GEN-2024/00293) [2025] NAHCMD 324 (20 June 2025)
Coram:	USIKU J
Heard:	13 February 2025
Delivered:	20 June 2025
Flynote:	Practice – Applications and motions – Eviction – Immovable property declared specially executable – Deputy Sheriff vested with statutory duty to pass transfer to a purchaser of the property sold in execution – Where the registered owner of the property frustrates the efforts of the Deputy Sheriff to do so, eviction of the registered owner is permissible in the circumstances – Eviction order granted.
Summary:	On 27 November 2018, this court granted an order declaring certain immovable property specially executable. On 10 May 2020, the property was placed under attachment and was sold in execution on 18 August 2022. Before transfer takes place, the purchaser of the property is required to obtain a building compliance certificate from the municipal council. Evidence on record shows that the purchaser is unable to obtain such certificate on account that the registered owner has threatened to shoot anyone who comes near the property for the purposes of enforcing the judgment debt in favour of the purchaser.
Held that where a registered owner of immovable property frustrates the efforts of a Deputy Sheriff from performing his statutory duties of passing transfer to a purchaser, an eviction order is permissible in the circumstances.
ORDER
The first respondent and all persons holding under him and their belongings, are ordered to vacate, within 7 days from the date of service of this order, the immovable property situated at a Unit consisting of:
Section No 7 as shown and more fully described on Sectional Plan No 32/2003, in the building(s) known as Schameerah Court situated at Hochland Park, in the Municipality of Windhoek, of which the floor area, according to the said Sectional Plan is 167 square metres in extent and;
(b)	an undivided share in the common property in the land and building(s) as shown and more fully described on the said Sectional Plan; (‘the property’).
2.	The applicant is directed to grant the purchaser of the abovementioned property vacant possession.
3.	The first and second respondents are ordered to pay the costs of the application, jointly and severally, the one paying the other to be absolved.
4.	The matter is removed from the roll and is regarded finalised.
JUDGMENT
USIKU J:
Introduction
[1]	This is an application for the eviction of the first respondent and all other persons holding under him and their belongings, from an immovable property described as a Unit consisting of:
Section No 7 as shown and more fully described on Sectional Plan No 32/2003 in the building(s) known as Schameerah Court situated at Hochland Park, in the Municipality of Windhoek, of which the floor area, according to the said Sectional Plan is 167 square metres in extent; and;
an undivided share in the common property in the land and building(s) as shown and more fully described on the said Sectional Plan; (‘the property’).
[2]	The application is brought by the applicant (the Deputy Sheriff for the District of Windhoek) against the first respondent, who is presently the registered owner of the property.
[3]	For the sake of convenience, I shall refer to the first respondent as the ‘the respondent’. The respondent opposes the application.
Background
[4]	On 27 November 2018, this court granted an order in favour of Standard Bank Namibia (‘the Bank’), among other things, declaring the property specially executable. The respondent has not appealed against that order.
[5]	On 10 March 2020, a writ of attachment was issued against the property and the property was duly attached.
[6]	On 18 August 2022, the property was sold in execution to the Bank.
[7]	The Bank, in compliance with its obligations in terms of the conditions of the sale, paid the purchase price and all other charges payable in terms of the agreement.
[8]	On 24 June 2024, the applicant brought the present application seeking the relief as more fully set out in paragraph 1 thereof.
The application
[9]	In his application, the applicant asserts that before the property may be transferred to the Bank, the local authority must issue a building compliance certificate in favour of the purchaser. The applicant avers that the purchaser has been unable to obtain a building compliance certificate, because the respondent has threatened to harm anyone that attempts to enforce the judgment debt on behalf of the Bank. According to the applicant, the respondent has informed him that he has a gun and that he will shoot anyone that comes near the property.
[10]	The applicant further states that the respondent continues to reside at the property despite the sale in execution and despite all efforts and requests by the purchaser. The respondent further refuses to give his cooperation and refuses to grant access to the immoveable property to the purchaser and the relevant authorities.
[11]	As a result of respondent’s conduct, says the applicant, the purchaser is unable to obtain transfer of the property, on account that the purchaser is unable to obtain the required building compliance certificate.
The respondent’s opposition
[12]	The respondent is a lay person and represents himself in this matter. In his answering affidavit, the respondent has not addressed any of the allegations made against him by the applicant.
[13]	Instead, the respondent asserts that the sale in execution was conducted unlawfully. He asserts that during the sale in execution, he was threatened by the applicant with a fire arm and that he subsequently opened a criminal case against the applicant.
[14]	The respondent further asserts that there is an ongoing appeal in the Supreme Court under case number SA 07/2023, stemming from case number HC-MD-CIV-MOT-GEN-2021/00304. According to the respondent, the appeal is still pending. It must be recorded that in case number HC-MD-CIV-MOT-GEN-2021/00304 the respondent sought leave to appeal against an order dismissing his application to represent certain body corporates. Furthermore, that case also concerns an order dismissing a recusal application which was instituted by the respondent. The appeal therefore has no relation to the present proceedings.
[15]	The respondent avers further that he has opened a criminal case against the applicant and the Bank over an ‘alleged organised judicial corruption syndicate’.
[16]	The respondent, therefore, requests that the present proceedings be stayed until his appeal and criminal cases are finalised.
Analysis
[17]	In the present matter, the applicant is obliged in terms of the provisions of rule 111(2) to give transfer of the property to the purchaser against payment of the purchase price and upon performance of the conditions of the sale. The evidence on record is that the applicant is unable to pass transfer to the purchaser on account of the conduct of the respondent, who has threatened to shoot anyone who comes near the property with the purpose of enforcing the judgment debt on behalf of the Bank. The evidence of the applicant in this respect is not disputed and the court therefore accepts it as factually correct.
[18]	The evidence on record is that, for the transfer to take place it is necessary to gain access to the property and allow municipal officials to conduct inspections necessary for the granting of the building compliance certificate. In the present case, this is not possible due to the conduct of the respondent.
[19]	The respondent has not placed before court what entitles him to continue occupying the property in the circumstances. Absent a court order reversing the order granted on 27 November 2018, which declared the property specially executable, there is no basis for the respondent’s challenge to the legality of the sale in execution.
[20]	Furthermore, the evidence in this matter shows that the respondent has prevented the applicant from performing his statutory duties to pass transfer of the property to the purchaser. This court has held on other occasions that where a registered owner of immovable property prevents the deputy sheriff from performing his statutory duties of passing transfer to a purchaser, eviction is permissible. I am bound to follow that authority, unless I can find that it is plainly wrong. On the evidence on record, I am satisfied that the applicant has established entitlement to the relief he seeks. I shall, therefore, grant the relief sought by the applicant.
[21]	In regard to the issue of costs, I do not find any special circumstances justifying a deviation from the general principle that costs follow the result. The general principle must therefore find application.
[22]	In the result, I make the following order:
1.	The first respondent and all persons holding under him and their belongings, are ordered to vacate, within 7 days from the date of service of this order, the immovable property situated at a Unit consisting of:
Section No 7 as shown and more fully described on Sectional Plan No 32/2003, in the building(s) known as Schameerah Court situated at Hochland Park, in the Municipality of Windhoek, of which the floor area, according to the said Sectional Plan is 167 square metres in extent; and;
(b)	an undivided share in the common property in the land and building(s) as shown and more fully described on the said Sectional Plan; (‘the property’).
2.	The applicant is directed to grant the purchaser of the abovementioned property vacant possession.
3.	The first and second respondents are ordered to pay the costs of the application, jointly and severally, the one paying the other to be absolved.
4.	The matter is removed from the roll and is regarded finalised.
